name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey seeks $100 million in additional school funding as districts confront mounting financial strain
description: Deploying a somewhat novel approach to budgeting "Fair Share" dollars, Gov. Maura Healey wants to give K-12 districts another funding injection amid rising economic pressures.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY on Wednesday proposed directing an additional $100 million to public school districts across Massachusetts, saying the funding would help communities manage growing financial challenges ahead of the new school year.
The proposal, which must be approved by the Legislature, would add to the more than $7 billion already appropriated for K-12 education in the fiscal 2027 state budget.
Districts would be able to use the funding based on their local needs, though Healey said the goal is to help schools avoid cuts to educational programs and reduce layoffs of teachers and other staff. 
The announcement comes as many districts continue to wrestle with shrinking enrollment, higher transportation expenses, and rising operating costs. Education groups, including the Massachusetts Teachers Association, have argued that state funding has not kept pace with inflation, leaving districts with difficult budget decisions.
“Cities and towns across Massachusetts are facing serious financial challenges, forcing school districts to make impossible choices,” Healey said during the announcement. “They’re considering layoffs, including teachers and paraprofessionals, cutting extracurricular activities and other mental health support services, all just in an effort to try to balance really tough budgets. This supplemental budget is meant to allow districts to respond to students’ needs and local needs.”
Massachusetts public schools are funded through a combination of state and local revenue. State education aid is primarily distributed through the Chapter 70 formula, which bases much of its funding on student enrollment. As enrollment declines, districts often receive less aid even though many of their expenses remain unchanged.
According to the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, statewide public school enrollment has fallen by more than 5 percent since fiscal 2019, a decline of nearly 50,000 students. The Massachusetts School Building Authority’s 2025 School Survey Report found the largest losses have occurred in smaller rural districts, while communities including Wareham, Sandwich, and Pembroke have also experienced enrollment declines of roughly 25 percent.
The fiscal 2027 budget increased Chapter 70 education aid by $300 million compared to last year. Under the funding formula, a minimum level of school spending is set for districts, with schools funded through a combination of local revenue and state aid. Each municipality’s required contribution is calculated using measures such as local property wealth and residents’ income.
This year also marks the final year of the phase-in of a six-year school funding reform law known as the Student Opportunity Act. Enacted in 2019, the law revised the state’s school funding formula by increasing funding for districts based on student needs. Schools serving larger numbers of English learners, low-income students, and students receiving special education receive additional per-pupil funding beyond the base amount.
The proposed supplemental funding would come from anticipated “Fair Share” surtax revenue, a voter-approved ballot initiative that placed a surtax on annual income above $1 million. Surtax revenue has already been used to expand several education initiatives, including free community college, universal free school meals, and child care grants.
The fiscal 2027 budget assumes the tax will generate approximately $2.7 billion, but collections have exceeded expectations in recent years. During fiscal 2026, for example, Surtax revenue surpassed the amount built into the budget by more than $700 million. Once final collections are certified later this year, the remaining surplus can be used for supplemental spending on public education and transportation.
State lawmakers typically wait until the final revenue haul for a cycle is clear before spending any extra collections. Healey’s proposal would instead make a portion of that anticipated surplus available before schools reopen, allowing districts to make staffing decisions sooner.
Healey’s new proposal would provide districts with an extra $112 in minimum per pupil aid, on top of money they’re already set to receive from the annual state budget, although the amount each district receives would depend on its 2027 enrollment. It would amount to a one-time injection that does not make any permanent changes to school funding formulas or tackle broader economic pressures facing schools.
While educators and advocates applauded the proposal, Christy Nickerson, president of the Woburn Teachers Association, noted that one-time funding cannot permanently resolve gaps created by declining enrollment and rising costs.
“While $100 million is significant, it will not be enough to fully counterbalance the challenges that our communities face,” Nickerson said. “Spiraling costs for healthcare and special education and the outdated limitations that Proposition 2½ [a law that limits the amount of revenue cities and towns can raise from local property taxes] place on municipalities are forcing cities and towns to make decisions that are not in the best interests of students and families.”
Policymakers might begin to weigh a response to longer-term pressure points as the funding increases laid out by the Student Opportunity Act finish taking effect. The annual state budget Healey signed last week reconvenes a commission that will explore the school funding formula, likely setting the scene for the next round of debate.
Erik Berg, president of the Boston Teachers Union, said more than 500 Boston Public Schools employees had been expected to lose their jobs before the upcoming school year. He said the additional funding could reduce the number of layoffs and urged lawmakers to act quickly so districts can restore positions before classes begin.
Additionally, Nickerson said the funding could help preserve educational opportunities that districts have struggled to maintain during recent budget cycles.
“It is imperative that these Fair Share funds be used to prevent cuts to student-facing positions and to save programs – from academics to the arts – that ensure our students are getting a comprehensive, well-rounded education,” she said.

title: Poor CHOOSE Act standards mean squandered taxpayer dollars
description: Summertime is fading. Not in the sense that we can expect crisp fall days any time soon, of course — we will be sweating our tails off for the foreseeable future. text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024. More than 34,000 Alabama students receive funds from the CHOOSE Act, which pays for nonpublic education expenses, including private school tuition and homeschooling. (Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Summertime is fading. Not in the sense that we can expect crisp fall days any time soon, of course — we will be sweating our tails off for the foreseeable future. But summer as it’s measured in the waxing and waning of the school calendar is indeed winding down.
In a few weeks, when Alabama’s K-12 students dust the beach sand from their feet and shuffle back into the classroom, more than 34,000 of their cohort will find themselves uplifted by a financial gift from the state: either $7,000 for school tuition (overwhelmingly at private schools) or $2,000 for homeschool materials, totaling more than $174 million in public funds. It’s equivalent to about 1.7% of the state’s 2027 education budget.
These are the lucky kids who applied for and were accepted into the CHOOSE Act program for 2026-27. This is the program’s second year, and also the last year that it includes a household income cap. If state lawmakers keep generously funding it — which they seem eager to do — next year ordinary taxpayers will chip in toward millionaires’ private school tuition. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Kay Ivey has pointed to the rising number of CHOOSE Act applications as evidence of the program’s popularity. 
Of course it’s popular. Who wouldn’t want free money? 
I’m certainly not going to begrudge any family a good education, whether they find it at a public school, private school, or homeschool. Every family has to find their own way. But underneath Ivey’s veneer of goodwill, it looks for all the world as though the CHOOSE Act is simply a convenient vehicle for lawmakers to rob public schools in order to fund minimally regulated Christian ones. 
The reality becomes inescapable if you review the list of participating schools: 79% of the private schools are Christian institutions. They come in every flavor, from Episcopal prep schools to Bible-loving, born-again Baptist schools. 
Mixing religion and education opens a Pandora’s box of conflicts that would not fly at a public school, from institutionalized discrimination against LGBTQ people to the kind of wackadoodle classroom instruction that pops up when science and Biblical literalism collide.
There are superficial measures in place to ensure that children are getting a quality education. For a school to become a CHOOSE Act participant, for example, it must either be accredited or pinky promise that it’s working on becoming accredited. 
But don’t let that fool you; not all accrediting bodies are created equal.
The state administrative code for the CHOOSE Act names two religious associations on the short list of approved accreditors. Both of them — the Alabama Christian Education Association (ACEA) and the American Association of Christian Schools (AACS) — push young Earth creationism, which asserts that God created the Earth in six days a mere 6,000 years ago, give or take. 
The AACS holds schools strictly to that line, requiring that each school they accredit be in harmony with the association’s statement of faith. The schools must teach young Earth creationism; school staff must affirm and support it; and curriculum choices must not deviate from it. 
Creationism leaks out into other areas of the CHOOSE Act, too. Several approved vendors on the list of classroom material providers specialize in creationist “science.” Among them: Apologia, BJU Press, Master Books, and Berean Builders Publishing. AL.com’s Rebecca Griesbach took a deep dive late last year into the CHOOSE Act’s myriad curriculum shortcomings.
If parents believe that the dinosaurs roamed the Earth alongside humans 6,000 years ago, it’s their prerogative to teach their kids as they see fit. But taxpayers shouldn’t cover the cost.
To be fair, in addition to the shaky accreditation provision, schools in the program must also conduct standardized testing once a year and report the results to the state. But they don’t have to hit a minimum achievement level; they just have to conduct the tests. Microschools — those with fewer than 20 students — are exempt from reporting their scores. (The list of participating schools includes 15 that identify as microschools.)
That’s about as deep as the scrutiny goes. If you run a microschool that’s “working on” becoming accredited, you pretty much just need a pulse, an address, a clean background check and a bank account, and you’re in. 
Politicians have tried to keep their hands clean from accountability, arguing that it’s the parents’ job to vet schools, not the state’s. And I have to hand it to them; they’ve committed to the bit, setting up the system so that no actual educators can meddle with it. 
The program is administered not by the State Department of Education, but by the Alabama Department of Revenue (ALDOR). ALDOR has done about as good a job as you could expect. They’re experts at handling money, not so great at vetting education providers. 
Ten of the 307 schools on their approved list don’t even appear to have websites.
Believe me, I’ve Googled the heck out of them. I think they do exist — I’ve found bits and pieces of evidence online — but either they’ve never bothered to put together a website, or they’ve let their subscriptions lapse. 
Another link on ALDOR’s list took me not to a school website, but to a sketchy website for a Russian casino. 
Having spent the better part of a week up to my neck in this stuff, I would like to request that we raise the bar at least an inch off the floor.
If the state of Alabama is indeed so flush with cash that our public schools couldn’t possibly use another cent, I think it’s reasonable to require some vetting of the private schools to which lawmakers are pushing excess funds. 
Approving anyone who’s capable of filling out an online form is a dereliction of duty. If a private school isn’t held to the same standards we hold for our public schools, there’s no reason on Earth — all 4.5 billion years of it — we should give them any of our hard-earned money.
